```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE, comment="#>", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE)
library(L0glm)
options(width=90, digits=3)
```

## Observation weights and offsets

`weights` describes observation contributions; `offset` supplies a known
contribution on the linear-predictor scale. Ordinary multichannel models accept
shared observation vectors or channel-specific matrices. Scalar weights and offsets
are expanded across observations and channels.

```{r weights}
set.seed(11)
X <- matrix(rnorm(300*12), 300, 12)
offset <- rep(log(2), 300)
y <- rpois(300, exp(.5 + .8*X[, 1] + offset))
fit <- L0glm.fit(X, y, family=poisson("log"), intercept=TRUE,
  weights=seq(.8, 1.2, length.out=300), offset=offset,
  lambda="gic", relaxed=TRUE, maxit=100)
predict(fit, X[1:3, ], offset=offset[1:3])
```

Multinomial models use observation weights with category-vector offsets.
Cox uses observation weights and one predictor offset per observation.
See the family tutorials for details.

## Nonnegative coefficients and mandatory terms

Set `nonnegative=TRUE` for a nonnegative fit. Intercepts are constrained too,
except that binomial and quasibinomial intercepts remain unrestricted.
`always.include` identifies predictor columns that remain eligible and unpenalized;
an added intercept is also unpenalized.

Eigen solvers enforce nonnegativity by clamping negative proposals to zero.
This works well in practice when the true active effects are positive and the
regularization level is well chosen, for example `lambda="gic"`. Ridge
shrinkage stabilizes the updates and often keeps genuine active effects positive.
OSQP quadratic programming and glmnet/`bigGlm` coordinate descent also provide
formally constrained ridge solves. In the package's
[deconvolution solver benchmarks](https://github.com/tomwenseleers/L0glm/blob/master/benchmarks/1_benchmarks_solvers_problem_sizes/metrics_all_conditions.csv),
Eigen Cholesky LLT generally gives better support recovery and coefficient
accuracy than these alternatives, together with much faster fits.
The native `L0nnpois()` backend specializes in nonnegative identity-link Poisson models.

## Starts and normalization

`start=NULL` uses a training-data ridge initializer. Scalar `start=1` initializes
ones in the normalized coefficient coordinates. Other explicit coefficient
vectors and matrices are interpreted on the original scale.

Explicit zero starts exclude the corresponding coefficients; rows that are
zero across all channels are omitted from the solves. Intercepts and
`always.include` terms remain eligible. Returned coefficients retain the
original dimensions. For multinomial models, starts are CLR-centered and
all-zero starting rows are excluded.

`normalize="auto"` uses RMS scaling for signed regression and preserves
the scale of a fully nonnegative design with a constrained intercept. An
unrestricted intercept permits implicit centering without densifying a sparse
matrix. Other choices are `"none"`, `"l2"`, `"rms"` and `"sd"`.
RMS scaling gives centered columns L2 norm \(\sqrt n\) when centering is used.
All coefficients are transformed back to the original scale.

## Dispersion

| `dispersion` | Behaviour for families with an estimated scale |
|---|---|
| `NULL` | Initialize and estimate the dispersion |
| A positive value | Keep the supplied value fixed |
| A negative value | Start at its absolute value, then estimate it |

Poisson and binomial dispersion is fixed at one. Negative-binomial shape uses
`mgcv::nb(theta=...)`; see its [tutorial](negative-binomial.html).

## Held-out early stopping

Validation selects a checkpoint during fitting. It is particularly useful when
prediction favours a point before the final sparse-selection iteration.
Coefficient updates continue to use training observations only.

```{r validation}
sim <- simul(n=300L, p=300L, n_nonzero=20L, m=4L, seed=7L)
set.seed(8)
v <- matrix(rpois(length(sim$y_true), sim$y_true), 300L, 4L)

validated <- L0nnpois(sim$X, sim$y, lambda="gic", ncores=2L,
  validation=list(X=sim$X, y=v, patience=3L, minit=3L))
validated$validation$deviance
validated$validation$selection$history
```

Here validation counts are an independent repeat measurement of the same latent
signals. In another application, pass a separate design and response.

The native Poisson backend scores validation deviance in C++, shares the design
across OpenMP workers and restores each channel's best checkpoint. Grouped
selection also retains the best shared-support pass. Relaxed refitting can keep
its initial selected coefficients when subsequent steps increase validation loss.

The default controls are `patience=3L`, `minit=3L` and `tol=1e-8`.
An improvement must exceed `tol * max(1, best_deviance)` to reset patience.
Validation weights and offsets follow the response formats; `mu_floor=1e-8`
is used only for positive-mean validation scoring. Diagnostics include
`selection`, `relaxed`, iteration histories and the selected start/batch candidate.

The same interface works through `L0glm.fit()` for all supported families.
`validation$rule="1se"` selects a simpler candidate within one empirical
standard error of the best candidate. Gaussian identity fits can compare default
and conditional marginal starts; an explicit `start` fixes that choice.

Use a separate test set to assess the model after selecting its stopping point.
